entries.title: BITCOIN FOUNDATION
entries.body:
Non-profit organization founded in September 2012. Its founding members are Gavin Andresen, Charlie Shrem, Mark Karpelès, Peter Vessenes, Roger Ver and Patrick Murck. Its objective was to promote the development of Bitcoin, to fund protocol developers and to represent the community before institutions.

In its early years, the foundation funded the work of developers such as Gavin Andresen and contributed to the standardization of the protocol. However, it was quickly confronted with controversies. Several of its founding members were subject to legal proceedings: Charlie Shrem was arrested in 2014 for money laundering linked to the Silk Road marketplace, and Mark Karpelès was indicted in Japan after the bankruptcy of Mt. Gox.

The foundation lost influence over the years, criticized for its governance and its lack of financial transparency. Part of the Bitcoin community reproached it for wanting to centralize the representation of a project designed to be decentralized.

entries.title: BRUTE FORCE ATTACK
entries.body: Cryptanalysis method for finding a password or a key, which consists of trying, by trial and error, all possible combinations of keys or passwords until finding the one that grants access to a privilege or to protected information. This technique relies on intensive computation and can be extremely long, especially against large keys. To deal with this type of attack, longer password and key sequences must be used in order to multiply the number of operations required for the attacker. In theory, the complexity of such an attack is exponential in the length of the target.

entries.title: F2POOL
entries.body: Bitcoin mining pool founded in April 2013 in China by Chun Wang and Mao Shixing ("Discus Fish"). F2Pool is the very first mining pool created in China and one of the oldest still operating in the world. It regularly ranks among the largest pools in terms of hashrate on the Bitcoin network, and caters to individual miners as well as professional mining infrastructures.

entries.title: FARADAY
entries.body: Tool developed by Lightning Labs, designed to extract data from an LND node and analyze it to assist its operator. It offers recommendations for closing underperforming channels and provides detailed information on the node's routing behavior. Faraday helps identify low-volume channels and those with availability (*uptime*) problems. This tool aims to assist node operators in allocating their capital across their channels.

entries.title: FAUCET
entries.body:
Website or application that gives away small amounts of bitcoin for free to its visitors, generally in exchange for solving a captcha or a simple task. The term "faucet" refers to the idea of dispensing currency drop by drop.

The first Bitcoin faucet was created by Gavin Andresen in June 2010 and distributed 5 BTC per visitor. In total, about 19,700 BTC were distributed by this site, with the aim of raising awareness of Bitcoin and encouraging its adoption at a time when the cryptocurrency had almost no market value.

Today, faucets exist mainly on test networks (testnet, signet), where they serve to provide test bitcoins to developers. On the main network, faucets have essentially disappeared because of the high value of bitcoin and the proliferation of bots.

entries.title: FEDERATION
entries.body:
Group of participants who collaborate to administer a network or a system, striking a compromise between centralization and decentralization. In a federation, responsibility is distributed among several independent entities rather than concentrated in a single one, which eliminates single points of failure and strengthens the system's resilience.

In the Bitcoin ecosystem, the federated model is used notably by the Liquid network, where a set of functionaries collectively sign blocks and manage the pegging operations (*peg-in* and *peg-out*) between the main chain and the sidechain. The Fedimint protocol also relies on a federated model to manage *Chaumian mints*. The concept of *Strong Federations*, formalized by Blockstream, describes a system in which functionaries operate under strict consensus rules, without requiring individual trust in each member.

entries.title: FEDIMINT
entries.body: Bitcoin payment and management protocol designed to improve privacy and reduce the demands placed on the main chain by pooling the custody of funds. Fedimint was created by Eric Sirion in 2021. It relies on a Chaumian bank system which, instead of being centralized around a single trusted actor, relies on federations. These federations are groups of trusted guardians who collectively hold and manage the bitcoins of the users in their group. Within the group, users can make payments with notes issued in exchange for their deposit of bitcoins. The idea behind Fedimint is to deploy this concept at the level of local communities. It is therefore a sort of evolution of the deposit bank based on bitcoin, with David Chaum's eCash system, and the use of a federation of trusted people in charge of the deposit and the issuance of the underlying asset.

entries.title: FEE BUMPING
entries.body:
Set of techniques that make it possible to increase the fees of a transaction already broadcast on the Bitcoin network in order to speed up its confirmation. When a transaction remains stuck in the mempools because its fees are too low relative to the demand for block space, fee bumping techniques make it possible to reassess its priority with miners.

The two existing methods are RBF (*Replace-By-Fee*) and CPFP (*Child Pays For Parent*). With RBF, the sender creates a new version of the original transaction with higher fees, which replaces the initial transaction in the mempools. With CPFP, the recipient (or the sender via a change output) creates a child transaction that spends an output of the stuck transaction, with fees high enough to incentivize miners to confirm both transactions together.

entries.title: FEE RATE - BITCOIN
entries.body:
Measure of the unit cost of the fees of a Bitcoin transaction, expressed in satoshis per virtual byte (sat/vB). The *fee rate* determines the priority of a transaction in the mempool: the higher the rate, the more miners are incentivized to include it quickly in a block. The absolute amount of fees corresponds to the difference between the total of the inputs and the total of the outputs of a transaction. The *fee rate* is obtained by dividing this amount by the weight of the transaction:
```math
fee\ rate\ (sats/vB) = \frac{frais\ (sats)}{poids\ (vB)}
```
This rate is freely chosen by the issuer of the transaction and works as an auction mechanism. During periods of congestion, the minimum *fee rate* for a transaction to be included in a block increases.

entries.title: FEE RATE - LIGHTNING
entries.body: Proportional component of routing fees on the Lightning Network. For each payment forwarded, a node can charge a *fee rate* calculated in proportion to the routed amount, expressed in parts per million (ppm). For example, a *fee rate* of 100 ppm means that the node charges 100 satoshis for every million satoshis routed. The *fee rate* complements the *base fee*, which is a fixed amount per transaction. Adjusting the *fee rate* is an essential lever in managing a routing node: a rate that is too high discourages traffic, while a rate that is too low does not offset the cost of tying up liquidity in the channel.

entries.title: FEE SNIPING
entries.body:
Attack scenario in which miners seek to rewrite a recently confirmed block in order to recover the transaction fees it contains, while also adding to it high-fee transactions that have arrived in the meantime in the mempool. The ultimate goal of this attack for the miner is to increase their profitability. *Fee sniping* can become increasingly profitable as the block reward decreases and transaction fees represent a larger share of miners' revenues. It can also be advantageous when the fees contained in the previous block are significantly higher than those of the next best candidate block. To simplify, the miner faces this choice in terms of incentives:
* Mine normally on top of the last block, with a high probability of winning a low reward;
* Attempt to mine an earlier block (*fee sniping*), with a low probability of winning a high reward.

This attack constitutes a risk for the Bitcoin system, because the more miners adopt it, the more the other miners, initially honest, are incentivized to do the same. Indeed, each time a new miner joins those attempting *fee sniping*, the probability that one of the attacking miners succeeds increases, and the probability that one of the honest miners extends the chain decreases correspondingly. If this attack is carried out on a massive scale and sustained over time, block confirmations would no longer be a reliable indicator of the immutability of a Bitcoin transaction. This could potentially render the system unusable. 

To counter this risk, most wallet software automatically fills in the `nLocktime` field so that it makes the validity of the transaction conditional on its inclusion at the next block height. Thus, it becomes impossible to include the transaction in a rewrite of the previous block. If widespread use of the `nLocktime` is adopted by Bitcoin users, this considerably reduces the incentives for *fee sniping*. Indeed, it encourages the progression of the blockchain rather than its rewriting by reducing the potential benefits of the latter. For Taproot transactions, BIP-0326 proposes using the `nSequence` field in a similar way to achieve the same effect as the `nLocktime` field for the other transaction types. This use would kill two birds with one stone by also improving the privacy of second-layer protocols that use this same field.

entries.title: FEE_ESTIMATES.DAT
entries.body: File in Bitcoin Core that stores estimated transaction fee data, compiled by the software from recent transactions and the current state of the mempool. These statistics help the user determine appropriate fees to include in their transactions so that they are confirmed in line with their expectations. This file has existed since version 0.10.

entries.title: FEELER CONNECTION
entries.body:
Ephemeral outbound connection that Bitcoin Core establishes every two minutes, once the 10 permanent outbound connections are filled (8 regular and 2 block-relay-only). It is limited to the `VERSION`/`VERACK` handshake to verify that an address does correspond to a reachable Bitcoin node, then closes.

The feeler connection alternates between two behaviors. If the eviction buffer contains addresses (the case of a collision during insertion into the "tried" table), it tests one of them: if the existing address responds, the new one is discarded; otherwise, the old one is replaced. This mechanism is called *test-before-evict*. If the buffer is empty, the feeler draws a random address from the "new" table and attempts to connect to it: if successful, the address is promoted to "tried".

This mechanism was introduced by Ethan Heilman as a countermeasure to certain types of eclipse attack. By populating the "tried" table with recently verified addresses, it reduces the proportion of obsolete addresses and makes it harder to eclipse a node. When no new block has been received for 30 minutes, Bitcoin Core detects a possible *stale tip* and establishes an additional outbound connection to a new peer, in order to check whether it has a more recent block and to bypass a possible network partition. This mechanism is distinct from feeler connections.

entries.title: FIAT
entries.body:
Currency, often state-issued, whose exchange value is imposed by public force.

*The term "fiat" is sometimes translated as "fiduciaire" although the latter term does not capture the dimension of legitimate violence that the term "fiat" embodies. In French, it is often accepted to use the English term "fiat" directly.*

entries.title: FIBRE
entries.body:
Acronym for "*Fast Internet Bitcoin Relay Engine*". It is a protocol designed by Matt Corallo in 2016 to speed up the propagation of Bitcoin blocks around the world. Its objective was to reduce propagation delays as close as possible to physical limits. FIBRE aimed to guarantee a fairer distribution of mining opportunities, by ensuring that the proportion of blocks mined by a participant faithfully reflects their contribution in terms of computing power, regardless of their position on the network.

Indeed, latency in block transmission can favor large groups of miners, well connected and often close to one another, to the detriment of smaller ones. This phenomenon could, in the long run, increase mining centralization and reduce the overall security of the system. To address this problem, FIBRE introduced error-correcting codes and the sending of additional data to offset packet loss, as well as the use of compact blocks similar to those described in BIP-0152, all operating over UDP to bypass certain limitations of TCP. Nevertheless, FIBRE was abandoned in 2020, mainly because of its dependence on a single maintainer and because the adoption of BIP-0152 made such a system less indispensable.

entries.title: FIDELITY BOND
entries.body:
Mechanism by which a user deliberately sacrifices bitcoin value to make a cryptographic identity costly to obtain, which deters Sybil attacks. The concept, initially proposed by Peter Todd in 2013, found its main application in JoinMarket, where it strengthens the privacy of coinjoins.

In JoinMarket, a *maker* who publishes a high-value *fidelity bond* has a greater probability of being selected by *takers* to participate in coinjoins, and therefore of earning fees. The most common way to create a *fidelity bond* is to send bitcoins to an address time-locked via a `OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY`. What is sacrificed is not the capital itself, but its time value: the bitcoins remain the property of the *maker*, but are immobilized until the lock expires. A long-term holder can thus build a *fidelity bond* at almost zero cost, since they did not plan to spend their bitcoins before the deadline.

An alternative consists of destroying bitcoins by sending them to a `OP_RETURN` output, making the sacrifice permanent and the proof trivial to verify.

entries.title: FINNEY HAL
entries.body:
Harold T. Finney II, known as Hal Finney, was a cryptographer and developer famous for his crucial role in the early days of Bitcoin and his contributions to cryptography. As soon as the Bitcoin White Paper was published in 2008, he was one of the first to interact with Satoshi Nakamoto. He gave feedback, reported bugs and proposed improvements after the software's launch in January 2009. He was the recipient of the first Bitcoin transaction (apart from coinbases), receiving 10 BTC from Satoshi in block no. 170:

```text
f4184fc596403b9d638783cf57adfe4c75c605f6356fbc91338530e9831e9e16
```

Hal Finney is also probably the first person, after Satoshi, to have mined a block: block no. 78. More than that, Hal Finney was the first promoter of Bitcoin during a period when the project was still little known.

Outside of Bitcoin, he is also recognized for his invention of RPoW (*Reusable Proofs of Work*), an electronic money system launched in 2004. Although RPoW did not meet with the expected success, it remains one of Bitcoin's most accomplished precursors. As a committed cypherpunk, Hal Finney also played a decisive role in the development and improvement of PGP (*Pretty Good Privacy*). Hal Finney left us on August 28, 2014, taken by amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Lou Gehrig's disease). He was cryopreserved by the Alcor foundation. He will remain a major figure in the history of cryptography and of Bitcoin.

entries.title: FLAG DAY
entries.body:
Soft fork activation method used in the early years of Bitcoin. This process simply defines a deadline date, known as the "*Flag Day*", before which the protocol upgrade must be adopted by the whole network. This approach is simple and direct: after this date, nodes and miners must have updated their software to comply with the new rules, failing which they risk finding themselves on an incompatible chain.

However, this method is very risky nowadays, because it requires significant coordination and consensus within the community, failing which the network may suffer a split, and the updated chain may not be the longest (with the most accumulated work). The *Flag Day* method can nevertheless be used for uncontroversial changes or urgent technical corrections.

entries.title: FLOOD AND LOOT
entries.body: Attack on the Lightning Network that exploits the HTLC mechanism to steal funds. It was described in 2020 by Jona Harris and Aviv Zohar. The attacker controls two nodes and opens channels with many intermediate victims. They route a large number of HTLCs from their source node to their target node through the victims, then refuse to reveal the preimage. As the *timelocks* approach expiry, all the victims are forced to unilaterally close their channels at the same time, which causes massive congestion of the blockchain. This congestion prevents some closing transactions from being confirmed in time. HTLCs not claimed before expiry revert to the attacker, who can bid up the fees thanks to RBF. Unlike *griefing*, which temporarily freezes funds without stealing them, *flood-and-loot* allows actual theft. The researchers estimated that about 85 channels attacked simultaneously are enough to guarantee a gain. The attack has never been observed in real-world conditions. The proposed countermeasures include reducing the maximum number of HTLCs per channel, adopting *anchor outputs* to dynamically adjust fees during a forced closure, and shortening expiry delays.

entries.title: FORCE CLOSE
entries.body:
Mechanism for the non-cooperative closure of a Lightning channel. When two users open a channel with a 2/2 multisig, each of them can unilaterally close the channel by broadcasting the latest commitment transaction, which is already signed, in order to recover their bitcoins *onchain*. In this case, we speak of a "*force close*".

This method is generally used if one of the participants no longer responds or if a cooperative closure of the channel is impossible. If a *force close* can be avoided, that is better, because it requires more time to recover one's funds *onchain* and can cost much more in fees.

During a *force close*, one of the two users broadcasts the commitment transaction that reflects the last known state of the Lightning channel. There is then a safety delay (*timelock*) before the bitcoins can be recovered *onchain*, which gives the other party time to verify that the transaction does correspond to the latest state of the channel. If a user attempts to cheat by publishing an outdated commitment transaction, the other party can use the revocation secret to punish the cheater and recover all of the channel's funds.

entries.title: FORCED ADDRESS REUSE
entries.body:
Attack that consists of sending tiny amounts of bitcoins to a large number of receiving addresses. The attacker's goal is to push the recipients to merge these amounts with other UTXOs. The attacker then tracks the future movements of these small amounts of bitcoins, with the aim of forming *clusters* of addresses, that is, determining whether several addresses belong to the same entity. By cross-referencing the information gathered during the attack with other data and heuristics used in chain analysis, it is possible for the attacker to identify certain entities and the associated addresses. This method represents a threat only to users' privacy, but does not affect the security of their funds.

*The original term for describing this attack is "Dusting Attack", but some bitcoiners suggest using the term "forced address reuse" instead, because they find the term "dust" inappropriate here.*

entries.title: FORFEIT TRANSACTION
entries.body:
Transaction by which a user of the Ark protocol cedes ownership of their input VTXO to the *Ark Service Provider* (ASP) during a round. Since the ASP advances the on-chain liquidity to create the new output VTXOs, it recovers in return the users' old VTXOs via these forfeit transactions.

The forfeit transaction exploits the forfeit clause (*forfeit clause*) written into the VTXO's policy, which consists of a multisig between the user and the ASP. Without an additional protection mechanism, signing this transaction would amount to giving up one's VTXO with no guarantee of getting a new VTXO in return. To solve this problem, a *connector output* from the round transaction is added as an additional input in the forfeit transaction. This link makes the transaction invalid as long as the round transaction is not confirmed on-chain, thus guaranteeing atomicity: the user loses their old VTXO only if the round's new VTXOs are actually created.

The forfeit transaction mechanism is also reused in the context of OOR (*out-of-round*) payments, where the forfeit clause is reused to transfer a VTXO directly to another user without going through a round.

entries.title: FORK
FORK - GIT
entries.body: In the context of Git, represents the creation of a copy of an existing repository on a new account, thus allowing the user to modify, test or develop the project independently of the original repository. Forks enable open source collaboration and contribution to projects without affecting the source repository.

entries.title: FOSS
entries.body: Acronym for "*Free and Open Source Software*". It refers to software under a license that allows anyone to run it for any purpose, to study it, to modify it to suit their needs, and to redistribute it freely, modified or not. This definition implies that the software's source code is publicly accessible.

entries.title: FOUNDATION DEVICES
entries.body: American company co-founded in 2020 by Zach Herbert, Jacob Johnston, Ken Carpenter and Matt Beach in Boston, specializing in the manufacture of open source hardware for securing bitcoins. Its flagship product, the Passport, is a hardware wallet (*hardware wallet*) operating in an air-gapped manner via QR codes and microSD cards, with no direct network connection. Foundation Devices also develops Envoy, a companion mobile application that serves as an interface for managing the Passport and interacting with the Bitcoin network. All of the hardware is assembled in the United States and the firmware is fully open source.

entries.title: FOUNDRY USA
entries.body: Bitcoin mining pool based in the United States, operated by Foundry Digital, a subsidiary of Digital Currency Group (DCG). Launched in 2020, Foundry USA Pool has become one of the largest mining pools in the world in terms of hashrate, regularly occupying first place. It provides mining services to institutional operators and to large North American mining farms. Foundry also offers financing, hardware purchasing and consulting services for professional miners. Foundry USA's predominance in the distribution of Bitcoin's hashrate raises questions about the geographic centralization of mining, with the majority of its computing power being concentrated in the United States.

entries.title: FOUNTAIN
entries.body: Podcast application integrating Lightning payments according to the *value-for-value* model. Founded in 2021 by Oscar Merry and Nick Malster, Fountain allows listeners to send micropayments in satoshis directly to content creators in real time while listening, via the Lightning Network. The application relies on the Podcasting 2.0 standard initiated by Adam Curry, which natively integrates Bitcoin payments into RSS feeds. Listeners can also earn satoshis by listening to podcasts, recommending content or interacting with the community. Fountain is available on iOS and Android.

entries.title: FPGA
entries.body:
Acronym for "*Field-Programmable Gate Array*". Integrated circuit that can be reconfigured after its manufacture to perform specific operations. Unlike conventional processors (CPUs), which are designed to be versatile, FPGAs allow the hardware logic to be programmed directly to adapt it to a precise task, which makes them more efficient in terms of energy consumption and performance for that task.

In the history of Bitcoin mining, FPGAs represented an intermediate stage between GPU mining and the arrival of ASICs. Starting in 2011, miners began using FPGAs to compute `SHA256` hashes, because they offered a better performance/power consumption ratio than GPUs, while remaining reprogrammable. The adoption of FPGAs was nevertheless relatively short, because ASICs, circuits entirely dedicated to `SHA256` hashing, quickly surpassed them in terms of computing power and energy efficiency.

entries.title: FPPS - FULL PAY PER SHARE
entries.body: Method of calculating miner remuneration in the context of mining pools. It is an evolution of the PPS (*Pay Per Share*) method. It pays miners not only for each valid share they submit, but also includes a portion of the transaction fees. The remuneration is calculated on the basis of the previous average transaction fees and the pool's hashrate. Thus, miners receive payment for the shares submitted, whether or not a block is found, but this method also pays for the expected value. It offers stable and predictable remuneration for miners, because it eliminates the variance linked to the probability of finding a block, while exposing them to fluctuations in the fee market. However, it is riskier for pool operators, because they must pay the miners even when no block is found, thus absorbing the variance risk.

entries.title: FROST
entries.body:
Schnorr threshold signature protocol proposed by Chelsea Komlo and Ian Goldberg in 2020, whose acronym stands for *Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold Signatures*. FROST optimizes the collaborative signing process by reducing it to two rounds of communication between participants, or even a single round when nonce preprocessing is performed.

The protocol relies on a (t, n) threshold scheme: among n participants who each hold a fragment of the private key, at least t of them must cooperate to produce a valid signature. The resulting signature is a standard Schnorr signature compliant with BIP-0340, indistinguishable from a signature issued by a regular payment. This property is particularly interesting in the context of Taproot, because it makes it possible to carry out multisignature operations on-chain without revealing the underlying threshold structure, which improves privacy and reduces transaction fees.

entries.title: FROSTSNAP
entries.body: Frostsnap is a security system for bitcoins based on the FROST protocol (*Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold Signatures*). Unlike classic multisig using Bitcoin script, FROST produces a single *on-chain* Schnorr signature, indistinguishable from a single-signature transaction, which improves privacy and reduces transaction fees. The Frostsnap team, made up notably of Nick Farrow and Lloyd Fournier, is developing dedicated hardware devices that connect in a chain via USB-C. The system makes it possible to add or remove signers after key generation, without changing the public address. The hardware and software are entirely *open source* under the MIT license.

entries.title: FULCRUM
entries.body:
Electrum server implementation developed in C++ by Calin Culianu, initially for Bitcoin Cash, and released under the GPLv3 license. Fulcrum indexes all the transactions of the Bitcoin blockchain from a full node and responds to queries from wallets compatible with the Electrum protocol.

Designed as a high-performance replacement for ElectrumX, Fulcrum uses a RocksDB database and takes advantage of the multithreaded and asynchronous programming of C++20 to offer fast response times, even under heavy load. It requires a Bitcoin Core (or Bitcoin Knots) node configured with `txindex=1` and without pruning.

The initial synchronization of the index with the blockchain takes much longer than with Electrs, and its storage currently approaches 200 GB. In return, it is significantly faster in use, whereas Electrs is slower, but stands out for its lightness.

entries.title: FULL RBF
entries.body:
Mempool policy that allows the replacement of any unconfirmed transaction by another transaction that spends at least one of the same inputs, but that offers a higher fee, regardless of whether the original transaction signaled its availability for replacement via the RBF *flag* (field `nSequence`). In classic RBF (opt-in RBF), only transactions that have explicitly enabled this signal can be replaced. Full RBF removes this restriction.

This policy was introduced in Bitcoin Core via the configuration option `mempoolfullrbf`, available starting with version 24.0 (November 2022) with a default value of `0` (disabled). Starting with version 28.0 (October 2024), this option was enabled by default (`mempoolfullrbf=1`), which makes Full RBF the standard behavior of Bitcoin Core.

Full RBF has been the subject of intense debate in the community. Its supporters argue that it improves the efficiency of the fee market and strengthens security by eliminating the false impression that transactions not signaling RBF would be irreversible before confirmation. Its opponents pointed out that it complicates use cases that relied on the acceptance of unconfirmed transactions ("zero-conf" transactions), notably in retail.

entries.title: FUNCTIONARIES
entries.body: In the context of the Liquid sidechain, functionaries are nodes operated by entities responsible for managing the system. They have two main roles: establishing consensus and executing transactions as block signers (*blocksigners*), and securing the bitcoins held by the network in order to ensure the two-way peg (*watchmen*).

entries.title: FUNGIBILITY
entries.body: Property of a currency that ensures that each unit is interchangeable and indistinguishable from another similar unit. Bitcoin, as a unit of account, is in principle fungible, because one bitcoin is always worth another bitcoin: 1 BTC = 1 BTC. However, the traceability of UTXOs (the medium of the units) on the blockchain can sometimes compromise this fungibility. Indeed, each satoshi can be distinguished by its history, which thus gives it a specific identity. The perception of the history of each UTXO can influence the parties' judgment on the fungibility of the bitcoins used. Thus, although fungibility is an intrinsic characteristic of monetary units, it can be altered by the specificities of the medium used for these units, as is the case with Bitcoin.

entries.title: HASH FUNCTION
MINING FARM
entries.body:
Facility where many mining machines (often ASICs) are grouped together to mine bitcoin by taking part in the proof-of-work process. The purpose of this grouping is to make it easier to manage the fleet of machines and to achieve economies of scale, notably for setup, maintenance, cooling, power supply and network connection. The mining farm also makes it possible to improve the proximity of the miners, and thus to reduce the latency that could affect their profitability.

*Note that the mining farm must not be confused with the mining pool.*

entries.title: TAGGED HASH FUNCTION
entries.body:
Variant of a hash function used in the Bitcoin protocol (notably in Taproot) to ensure domain separation. A tagged hash function takes a tag (a UTF-8 character string) and data as input, and computes the hash as follows:
```math
TaggedHash(tag,\ data) = SHA256(SHA256(tag)\ \Vert\ SHA256(tag)\ \Vert\ data)
```
Prefixing the data with the double hash of the tag ensures that hashes computed in different contexts cannot collide. For example, a hash computed with the tag `TapLeaf` can never be identical to a hash computed with the tag `TapBranch`, even if the data is the same.

This mechanism was introduced by BIP-0340 and is used across all the BIPs related to Taproot (BIP-0341 and BIP-0342). Each step in the construction and spending of a P2TR output uses a distinct tag: `TapLeaf` for the leaves of the script tree, `TapBranch` for the branches, `TapTweak` for the tweak calculation, and `TapSighash` for the creation of the signature hash. BIP-0340 also uses tags for Schnorr signatures: `BIP0340/challenge`, `BIP0340/aux` and `BIP0340/nonce`.

entries.title: TRANSACTION FEES
entries.body:
Transaction fees represent an amount intended to compensate miners for their participation in the proof-of-work mechanism. These fees incentivize miners to include transactions in the blocks they create. They are the result of the difference between the total amount of the inputs and the total amount of the outputs of a transaction:

```text
frais = inputs - outputs
```

They are expressed in `sats/vBytes`, which means that the fees do not depend on the amount of bitcoins sent, but on the weight of the transaction. They are freely chosen by the sender of a transaction and determine its speed of inclusion in a block through an auction mechanism. For example, imagine that I make a transaction with an input of `100 000 sats`, an output of `40 000 sats` and an output of `58 500 sats`. The total of the outputs is `98 500 sats`. The fees allocated to this transaction are `1 500 sats`. The miner who includes my transaction will be able to create `1 500 sats` in their coinbase transaction in exchange for the `1 500 sats` that I did not recover in my outputs. 

Transactions with higher fees, relative to their size, are processed with priority by miners, which can speed up the confirmation process. Conversely, transactions with lower fees may be delayed during periods of heavy congestion. It should be noted that Bitcoin transaction fees are distinct from the block subsidy, which is an additional incentive for miners. The block reward is composed of the new bitcoins created with each mined block (block subsidy), as well as the collected transaction fees. While the block subsidy decreases over time due to the limitation of the total supply of bitcoins, transaction fees will continue to play a crucial role in encouraging miners to participate. 

At the protocol level, nothing prevents users from including transactions with no fees in a block. In reality, this type of fee-free transaction is an exception. By default, Bitcoin nodes do not relay transactions with fees below `1 sat/vBytes`. If some fee-free transactions have gotten through, it is because they were included directly by the winning miner, without traveling across the network of nodes. For example, the following transaction includes no fees:

```text
fd456524104a6674693c29946543f8a0befccce5a352bda55ec8559fc630f5f3
```

In this specific example, it was a transaction initiated by the director of the F2Pool mining pool. As a normal user, the lower limit is therefore currently `1 sat/vBytes`.

The purge limits must also be taken into account. During periods of heavy congestion, nodes' mempools purge their pending transactions below a certain threshold, in order to respect their allocated RAM limit. This limit is freely chosen by the user, but many leave the default Bitcoin Core value of 300 MB. It can be modified in the `bitcoin.conf` file with the `maxmempool` parameter.

entries.title: TRANSACTION FINALITY
entries.body: Concept that designates the moment from which a transaction is considered irreversible and permanently recorded in the blockchain. On Bitcoin, finality is probabilistic rather than absolute: each new block added on top of the block containing the transaction makes reversing it exponentially more difficult and costly. By convention, a transaction is generally considered final after 6 confirmations, or about one hour, because the probability that an attacker could reorganize the chain, or that a natural fork would reach such a depth, is extremely low. However, for modest amounts, one or two confirmations may be deemed sufficient.
